Subject: Performance SLO follow-up: context window & latency impact

Hi Sam / Jared —

Great to meet you both this morning. Quick recap from our discovery call and proposed next steps (see attachments: FinCo-SLO-template.xlsx, sample_payloads.json).

Summary of what we heard from FinCo: 
- Latency target: p95 <= 250 ms for the primary user flow (real-time recommendations).
- Peak concurrency target: 60 concurrent requests; typical concurrency ~20.
- Expected throughput: ~10k requests/day with burst windows during business hours (~1.5x).
- Streaming requirement: yes — progressive responses for the recommendation stream are required for perceived latency improvements.
- Context window: ingest up to ~32k tokens for long user histories (input); expected output up to ~2k tokens.

Why context window matters for latency (brief):
- Bigger context windows increase memory and KV cache size per request, which can increase per-token generation latency and GPU memory pressure.
- For autoregressive models, longer input means longer KV lookup/management and larger state to pass through the runtime; that can increase tail latency unless mitigations are used (prefix caching, chunked encoding, or retrieval-augmented approaches).

Initial recommendations (what Redwood would do):
1) Model & versioning: start with an open LLM variant tuned for generation with 32k context support; we can propose a quantized variant to reduce memory and improve throughput.
2) Streaming + partial outputs: enable streaming so frontend can render partial recommendations while generation continues; reduces perceived latency even if total generation time is non-trivial.
3) Batching policy: continuous batching with a tight max-wait (e.g., 5–15 ms) to balance throughput and tail latency. This typically keeps p95 low while still reducing cost.
4) Context handling: evaluate prefix caching for repeated prefixes (user metadata), and consider chunking long histories server-side to only include the most relevant context for generation.
5) Concurrency slots & autoscaling: reserve dedicated concurrency slots for the realtime flow up to the peak concurrency target while using autoscaling for the remainder.

Open items / asks for the technical deep-dive:
- Sample payloads for the 32k-token case (thanks for sharing a sanitized example in sample_payloads.json).
- Clarify SLOs for streaming UX (e.g., time-to-first-byte target).
- Any infra constraints (VPC/on-prem requirements).

Next steps:
- I'll schedule a technical deep-dive where we bring infra + runtime engineers (propose Tue 5/26 or Wed 5/27).
- Please review the attached SLO template and update the values where you can.

Thanks — talk soon.
—Marissa

Sam — great questions. Below are pragmatic, experience-backed answers and the trade-offs we've seen: 

1) Context window (8k -> 32k) impact on p95: 
- Ballpark: on the same model family, raw generation p95 can increase by ~20–60% depending on how much of the long context affects attention scope (worst at long sequences where attention cost grows). In practice: 8k context p95 = 180–220 ms; 32k context p95 = 260–360 ms (numbers vary by model size and runtime kernels).
- Mitigation: prefix caching (for repeated prefixes) and model-side chunking can bring p95 closer to the 8k baseline for many requests.

2) Batching vs streaming: 
- Batching helps throughput but introduces queuing latency. For continuous batching with a tight max-wait window (5–15 ms), the added latency is small and often acceptable for p95 targets. If you batch aggressively (50–100 ms windows), p95 will increase accordingly and will hurt time-to-first-token.
- For streaming where time-to-first-token is critical, we recommend a hybrid: keep max-wait very low for the realtime route (<=15 ms) and allow larger batch windows on background/off-peak routes.

3) Cost delta (32k vs 8k): 
- Larger context increases compute per request (memory ops + KV management). Expect unit cost to increase roughly proportional to the extra tokens processed and memory bandwidth — typically 1.5x–2x higher on large contexts unless you use quantization and efficient kernel paths. 
- Retrieval + 8k approach often lowers cost while preserving quality if you can index relevant context and send only the top-k retrieved chunks. There is an engineering cost to maintain the retrieval layer.

4) Time-to-first-token <= 120 ms at p95 with 32k: 
- It's challenging but sometimes achievable with tuned runtime and reserved concurrency slots. The biggest lever is ensuring the first token path is unblocked: small batch windows, streaming enabled, and pinned resources for realtime flow. If you need hard 120 ms p95 across the board, we generally recommend either reducing client-visible context or reserving dedicated low-latency nodes for that critical route.

Proposed tactical next steps for the deep-dive (we'll bring infra + runtime engineers):
- Run a short benchmark with your sample payloads: 8k vs 32k, measure time-to-first-token, p50/p95, and memory.
- Test streaming behavior with small batch windows (5 ms, 15 ms, 50 ms) to show trade-offs.
- Evaluate retrieval + 8k prototype on one user cohort (compare quality + cost).

Scheduling: confirm Tue 5/26 3:00pm PT / Wed 5/27 10:00am PT and we'll send calendar invite with a benchmark plan.

I'll attach a short benchmark checklist to the calendar invite.
